feedback: If the child names a part but not its job, prompt: 'What would the rover use its wheels (or cameras, or drill) FOR on Mars?'
Affirm when the child links the drill to studying rocks and the cameras to seeing/avoiding danger.

If the child says the rover is hunting living aliens, correct gently: it looks for CLUES in the rocks that water once flowed and that tiny life could ever have existed — evidence, not creatures walking about.
activities.intendedInsight: A rover is a real machine whose parts each have a job, and together those jobs let it explore Mars and search for evidence of past water and life.
learnerActions: Look at a labelled picture of a real rover (Curiosity or Perseverance) sitting on rusty, rocky Mars terrain.

Point to each part and say its job: chunky wheels — 'built to climb over rocks'; camera mast — 'its eyes: to look around and spot danger'; robotic arm and drill — 'to study what the rocks are made of' (a camera on the arm is also what takes the rover's famous selfies).
Point to a drilled rock and explain the purpose: the rover is 'looking for signs that water was once here, and maybe tiny life long ago'.
Say the rover's name and one signature fact about it.
activities.title: Explore the rover and its jobs on a Mars scene

feedback: If the child gives only rocket size as the reason, list the real reasons together: months of travel, no breathable air, dangerous radiation, high cost, and no risky return needed — a robot can simply stay and work.
Affirm answers that name two or more genuine hazards (distance, air, radiation).
Ask the child what a robot does NOT need on Mars that a human astronaut would need (air, food, water, a return trip).
activities.intendedInsight: Robots are our stand-ins in places too hostile and too far for humans right now; their data also helps design safer future human missions.
learnerActions: Consider the question: 'Why do we send a robot rover instead of a person to Mars?'

Build a reasons-list tied to Mars being hostile: it is very far away (the journey takes many months), there is no breathable air (the atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide, not oxygen), and there is dangerous radiation.
Add that a robot can stay and work for years, needs no air, food, or return trip, and keeps humans safe.
Explain why 'we just can't build a big enough rocket' is NOT the main reason — the real barriers are distance, no air, danger, and cost.
activities.title: Why send a robot, not a person?

feedback: If a part-to-job match is wrong, revisit the labelled rover picture.
If the child picks rocket size as the main reason, re-list the real reasons (distance, no air, radiation, cost, no return).
If the child says the search is for living aliens, restate that it is a search for evidence of past water and possible ancient life.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can recall and organise the key facts: rover names, parts-to-jobs, and the genuine reasons for robotic exploration.
learnerActions: Match each rover part to its job (wheels → drive over rocks; cameras → see and photograph; drill/instruments → study rocks).
Sort rover jobs into categories: drive, photograph, drill, and search for evidence.
Choose the real reasons we send a robot instead of a person (far away, no breathable air, dangerous radiation) and set aside the weak reason (rocket size as the only cause).
Name a rover and state one job it does.
activities.title: Check and sort what you know
